candidate_findings.message: Declare the pytest plugins required by the new test. The declared development dependencies contain neither `pytest-mock` nor `pytest-asyncio`. In an environment installed from this project's dependencies, the new test fails because the `mocker` fixture is unavailable; asynchronous execution also requires the asyncio plugin. Add both plugins to the development dependencies and lockfile.

Call the patched avatar loader through its module. Patching `chat_interface._load_avatar_infos_for_chat` does not replace the function already imported into this test's namespace. This call therefore executes the real loader against `DB_PATH`, potentially creating or reading the production database and failing when avatar settings are absent. Use `chat_interface._load_avatar_infos_for_chat()` to invoke the configured mock.

Exercise the real chat handler rather than the mocked dependency. This invokes the same `send_request_to_open_ai` mock whose side effect supplies every asserted result and updates history. Consequently, the test never executes `send_request_to_llm` and passes even if that handler's prompt construction, history update, or video orchestration is broken. Call the real handler, mock the LLM to return response text, and mock the voice-generation dependency as well.

This test never runs any real code. `send_request_to_llm`, the function that handles the chat interaction, is never called. Instead the test calls `chat_interface.send_request_to_open_ai`, which it replaced with a mock just above. The mock's side effect appends to CHAT_HISTORY and returns a hard-coded tuple, and the asserts then check that same tuple and list. The test passes no matter how `send_request_to_llm` behaves, so it gives no coverage of the chat flow or the history handling it claims to test. Call `await chat_interface.send_request_to_llm(...)` and mock only its external dependencies: `send_request_to_open_ai`, `send_request_to_elevenlabs`/`send_request_to_zonos` and `send_request_to_generate_video`.

The mock doesn't match the real `send_request_to_open_ai` (fetcher/fetching.py:7). The real function takes a single `messages` list and returns the LLM text response. The mock is called with 10 positional args and returns the `(msg, history, video)` tuple that `send_request_to_llm` returns. Because the mock has no spec, the signature mismatch goes unnoticed. If this mock were used against the real caller, `text_response` would be a tuple. Have it return a plain string, and use `autospec=True` so the signature is checked.

The PR says it adds two tests, one for ElevenLabs and one for Zonos, but there is only one test. Neither `send_request_to_elevenlabs` nor `send_request_to_zonos` is mocked or checked. Use `pytest.mark.parametrize` over `voice_model` ('elevenlabs', 'zonos'), call the real `send_request_to_llm`, and assert that the matching voice function was awaited with the right arguments.

`_load_avatar_infos_for_chat` is imported directly into the test module at line 2, so the later `mocker.patch("aafactory.chat.interface._load_avatar_infos_for_chat", ...)` doesn't affect that local name. Line 39 therefore calls the real function, which opens the real TinyDB at DB_PATH. On a clean checkout or in CI, `avatar_page_settings_table.get(doc_id=1)` can return None, and `.get("avatar_name")` on None raises AttributeError. The test then depends on a developer's local DB, which may be why it only passes locally. Call it through the module (`chat_interface._load_avatar_infos_for_chat()`) or skip it and build the inputs directly.

The test needs the `mocker` fixture from pytest-mock and `@pytest.mark.asyncio` from pytest-asyncio, but pyproject.toml lists only pytest and pytest-cov as dev dependencies. On a fresh install, `mocker` won't be found and the async test won't run (it is skipped or fails with 'async def functions are not natively supported'). Add `pytest-mock` and `pytest-asyncio` to `[tool.poetry.group.dev.dependencies]`.

CHAT_HISTORY is cleared at the start of the test but never reset afterwards, so the global state is left behind for later tests. Use an autouse fixture, or `mocker.patch.object(chat_interface, 'CHAT_HISTORY', [])`, so each test starts and ends with an empty history. That is the isolation the PR description promises.

The description says print statements were added for debugging, but this diff has none, so the description doesn't match the change. If prints are added, prefer asserts or pytest's `-s`/logging over leaving them in the tests.

The User Guide no longer matches what the command does. Line 335 still says notes 'will be persisted in future milestones' and that the command only 'validates syntax', and line 360 says `note` is not undoable. This PR makes notes persistent and undoable. The guide also still documents `note d-/DATE` (lines 342-349 and the summary table at line 439), but `NoteCommandParser` does not handle `d-/`, and this PR removes the delete format from `MESSAGE_USAGE`. Users who follow the guide will get a format error. Update the note section and remove or flag the delete-note entries.

`model.setNote` calls `Map.put`, so a second `note` for the same date silently replaces the earlier note. The success message still says 'New note recorded', and the user is never told that the previous note was lost. Since there is no delete or edit command, overwriting is the only way to change a note, and it happens without any notice. Do one of the following: append to the existing note, report the replacement in the result message (for example 'Note for X updated, previous note: ...'), or reject duplicates.

Notes are serialised through a `HashMap`, while `AddressBook` uses a `LinkedHashMap` so that merged planner notes keep their insertion order (the ModelManagerTest comment relies on this). After a save and reload, the order is the `HashMap`'s order. As a result, the merged note shown for a date (for example 'everyday' plus a specific date) can appear in a different order after the app restarts. Use a `LinkedHashMap` here, in both the field and the deserialisation path.

Two different JSON keys can parse to the same `VisitDate`, because `VisitDate.of` lowercases its input. For example, 'e-TUESDAY' and 'e-tuesday' from a hand-edited file both become the same date, and `setNote` silently keeps whichever one the `HashMap` returns last. Detect the collision and either reject it (as is done for duplicate locations) or merge the two notes, so that data is not dropped without warning.

Matching notes are joined into one `NoteContent` with only blank lines between them, so the planner does not show which date each part came from (for example 'Every Tuesday' versus '24 Mar 26'). This becomes a real problem because there is no delete command: users cannot tell which date to overwrite in order to change a given part. Consider prefixing each part with its `VisitDate` label.

The new `equals` and `hashCode` tests only check reflexivity and a non-`AddressBook` argument. None of them shows that two address books with the same locations but different notes are unequal. That is the behaviour this PR changes, and undo/redo depends on it: `commitState` compares `AppState` snapshots, so if `equals` ignored notes, a `note` command would not be recorded for undo. Add a test with different notes, and an undo/redo test for `NoteCommand`.

Execute the converted routine in the Rust benchmark. The generated benchmark comments out the routine call and times only `black_box` on a reference. Consequently, even a correct conversion receives a speedup comparing actual Fortran computation against an effectively empty Rust loop. Import and invoke the converted function inside the timed loop before reporting performance ratios.

Do not pass accuracy checks without a Rust comparison. When the Rust crate fails to build, the pipeline passes `crate_dir=None`, yet this branch marks accuracy as passed whenever the Fortran reference runs. Rust compilation failures and output-length mismatches therefore produce successful accuracy results without validating any converted output. Treat uncompleted comparisons as failed or explicitly skipped rather than passed, including cases where only some test cases complete.

Exclude the C function's outer braces from the Rust body. When f2c succeeds, the body loop translates and retains the C function's closing `}`, then this code appends another closing brace for the Rust wrapper. For a single-line C signature this produces an unmatched closing delimiter; multiline signatures also leak their remaining parameter declarations into the body. Parse the complete C signature and outer body boundary before translating statements, otherwise the default hybrid path cannot produce compilable Rust without LLM intervention.

Include the console entry point module in distributions. `find_packages()` includes the `fortran_to_rust` packages but not the top-level `convert.py` module. A regular wheel installation therefore installs a `fortran-to-rust` command that raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'convert'` outside the checkout. Include `convert` through `py_modules` or move the entry point into the installed package.

The f2c→Rust skeleton is broken in two ways. For SUBROUTINEs, f2c writes the prototype as `/* Subroutine */ int dgemm_(...`, but `_c_to_rust` drops every line that starts with `/*`. As a result `in_body` never becomes true and the output is an empty stub. For FUNCTIONs such as ddot, dasum, dnrm2 and idamax, the prototype line survives, so raw C is copied in almost verbatim: `static integer ...;`, pointer derefs like `*n` on by-value i32 params, the C function's own `{`/`}` plus ours, and `return ret_val;` followed by the `0.0` default. That code cannot compile. f2c is installed in the devcontainer and Hybrid is the default strategy, so any FUNCTION in the selection breaks `cargo build` for the whole crate.

Hybrid always returns `success=True`, even when the result is an empty or TODO stub that does nothing, or C-ish code that doesn't compile. The report and CLI then show these functions as "✅ OK" or converted, which hides that nothing was actually translated.

The LLM polish output is used as-is. It is not passed through `_strip_fences` or `_ensure_top_level_pub_fn`, and it is not compile-checked. Markdown fences, prose, a renamed or `mod`-wrapped function, or `char` instead of `u8` all go straight into the crate. The polish prompt doesn't require the `pub fn {name}` signature or u8 CHARACTER args either.

`success=True` is reported even when the code still fails `cargo check` after all repair rounds. That module is still written into the crate, so one bad function makes `cargo build` fail for every function and blocks all accuracy and benchmark checks. Meanwhile the report shows the function as OK.

The idiomisation (polish) pass runs after the compile/repair loop, and its output is never re-checked. `_ensure_top_level_pub_fn` is also never applied in this strategy. Code that compiled can be replaced with code that doesn't (or with a renamed or wrapped function), and the result is still marked `success=True`.

If no Rust output was compared (no crate, Rust build failed, length mismatch on every test, or the routine prints nothing), the result is still `passed = fortran_ok_count > 0`. The Markdown and HTML reports and convert.py then show ✅ for accuracy even though no comparison happened. Earlier exits (around lines 673–695) also return `passed=True` when the routine can't be resolved. A failed or skipped comparison should not count as a pass.

For FUNCTIONs, the Rust example prints the return value first and the arrays after. The Fortran driver does the opposite: it prints the arrays first and appends the result last (line 471). For functions with array args like DDOT or DASUM, the outputs are compared at the wrong positions, so a correct translation is reported as FAIL with a large error.

`is_real` treats REAL the same as DOUBLE PRECISION, and `_TYPE_PATTERNS` has no COMPLEX entry. COMPLEX args fall back to a DOUBLE PRECISION scalar. Drivers for DSDOT (REAL SX/SY) and DZASUM/DZNRM2 (COMPLEX*16 arrays), which are all in BLAS_FUNCTIONS, therefore pass the wrong types or shapes, and the Fortran reference results are garbage or the run crashes.

Every `*` or unknown dimension resolves to 4. Packed arrays (AP(*) for DSPMV/DTPMV/DSPR need N*(N+1)/2 = 10) and banded LDA requirements (DSBMV/DTBMV need LDA ≥ K+1 with K=4) are under-sized. That causes out-of-bounds access in the Fortran reference or an XERBLA STOP, so these routines are never meaningfully tested.

Only real arrays are printed and compared. Scalar outputs (for example DROTG's DA, DB, C, S and DROTMG's scalars) are never checked, and the Rust example passes those scalars by value. Routines whose only outputs are scalars end up with 0 vs 0 values and are reported as passed without any check.

The Rust benchmark never calls the converted function; the call is commented out and only `black_box(&array)` runs. The reported Rust time is an empty loop, so the 'Rust is Nx faster than Fortran' speedup in the report and summary is fabricated.

10 reps at 4×4 sizes timed with `CPU_TIME` is usually below the timer's resolution, so it typically measures 0.0 ms. `summary` and the report check `fortran_time_ms` for truthiness, so 0.0 shows as N/A or 'Incomplete'. Benchmarks need realistic sizes or adaptive repetition counts.

The `subprocess.run` calls for gfortran, cargo and the built executables don't catch `FileNotFoundError` or `TimeoutExpired`. The same applies in benchmarker.py `_run_fortran_bench`/`_run_rust_bench` and rust_project.py `quick_check`/`build_crate`/`test_crate`. On a local setup without gfortran, or after a slow cargo build, the whole pipeline crashes with a traceback after conversion instead of reporting a skipped check.

All converted modules go into one crate unconditionally, so a single module that fails to compile makes `build_ok` False. Callers then pass `crate_dir=None` to accuracy and benchmark for every function. With 10+ functions, one bad translation blocks validation of all of them. Consider excluding modules that fail `quick_check`, or validating each function on its own.

`scaffold_crate` reuses an existing crate directory without clearing `examples/` or old `src/*.rs`. On a re-run, stale `accuracy_*.rs`/`bench_*.rs` examples for functions that are no longer in the crate, or whose signatures changed, get compiled by `cargo test` and make it fail.

The prompt context tells the LLM that `lsame(ca: u8, cb: u8) -> bool` and `xerbla(&str, i32)` exist, but the crate and the `quick_check` snippet never provide them. The LLM will call undefined functions (E0425) and spend its repair rounds on that. Either provide these helpers in the crate or tell the LLM to define them inline.

The indexing guidance contradicts itself: it says 'Convert to 0-based row-major' and in the same sentence says column-major is kept (`a[j*lda+i]`). The harness feeds column-major data, so any row-major translation will fail the accuracy check.

`_ensure_top_level_pub_fn` only fixes a bare `fn name` at column 0. `unsafe fn name`, `pub(crate) fn name`, and indented or `mod`-wrapped definitions are left alone, so the E0425 problem it targets can still happen.

The primary GitHub source builds the URL with `fn.upper()` (e.g. `DGEMM.f`), but files in Reference-LAPACK/lapack/BLAS/SRC are lowercase (`dgemm.f`). Every GitHub download 404s, and the code always falls back to plain-HTTP netlib (line 41). That means unauthenticated, MITM-able source that is then compiled and executed.

Tarball extraction only checks member paths, not symlink or hardlink targets. A link member can still write outside `output_dir`; use `extractall(filter='data')` on Python ≥ 3.12. Also, `output_dir.rglob('*.f')` includes files already in the cache, so `shutil.copy2` raises SameFileError. The bare `except` then returns False partway through copying.

A failed or truncated download (≤100 bytes, or an exception after a partial write) leaves `dest` on disk. Later runs treat any existing `{fn}.f` as cached, and `fetch_blas` returns it in `result`, so a corrupt file is used permanently.

`is_available` requires an API key. With `LLM_PROVIDER=openai_compatible` and a local Ollama/LM Studio server that needs no key (the README marks the key as optional), the client counts as unavailable, and Strategies 1 and 2 silently fall back to Hybrid.

The client silently reads the Copilot extension's `oauth_token` from `~/.config/github-copilot/hosts.json` and sends it to a third-party endpoint. That token belongs to another app, and using it without telling the user is a credential-handling concern. Also, if `LLM_BASE_URL` is set while the provider is github_models (lines 176–178), the auto-discovered GitHub token is sent to that arbitrary URL.
On HTTP 429, the code sleeps for the server-supplied `Retry-After` with no cap. If every attempt gets a 429, `last_exc` is still None, so the raised error reads 'failed after N attempts: None'.

convert.py has its own .env loader that runs first and doesn't strip quotes. `LLM_API_KEY="abc"` gets stored with the quotes, and because `llm_client._load_dotenv` only sets missing keys, the quoted value is what gets used, so authentication fails.

The console script points to `convert:main`, but `convert.py` is a top-level module that `find_packages()` doesn't include, and `py_modules` isn't declared. A non-editable install creates a `fortran-to-rust` command that fails with ModuleNotFoundError.
`open_browser` defaults to True, and convert.py's `--non-interactive` (CI) path doesn't override it, so headless and CI runs try to launch a browser.

Args are taken only from the first header line. A SUBROUTINE or FUNCTION header continued onto the next line (allowed in fixed-form) gets an empty or truncated arg list, which breaks driver, signature and accuracy generation for that routine.

`_result as f64` doesn't compile for LOGICAL functions (bool can't be cast to f64), and the Fortran side prints `(L5)` T/F, which `float()` can't parse. LOGICAL-returning functions can never be compared.

The 'sample' scope uses `BLAS_FUNCTIONS[:n]`, which with the default of 10 is all Level-1 routines and excludes dgemm, the primary milestone target. The curated `BLAS_SAMPLE` list is defined but never used.

The 'Questioner' is a fixed set of keyword-triggered questions, not an LLM reviewing the draft (`rust_draft` is unused). The 'IMPLICIT' check also fires for every BLAS routine, since they declare all variables explicitly but don't contain IMPLICIT NONE. This doesn't deliver the Questioner–Solver behaviour described.

The GET download route (consumer controller line 353, and the matching one at publisher publish.ts:761) reads `req.query.download_language` and only casts it with `as Locale`; it never validates it. Before this change, a bad value ended up in a `lang` query param that `fetch` then overwrote, so it had no effect. Now `language as Locale` is sent unchecked as the `Accept-Language` header and the `lang` query param. A crafted URL (an unsupported locale, or a value with characters that aren't legal in a header) now reaches the backend or makes `fetch` throw, which returns a 500. Validate against `Object.values(Locale)` and fall back to `req.language`, or type the `language` parameter as `Locale` and validate at the route, instead of hiding the problem with a cast.

The same fix is applied to the publisher preview download (`downloadDatasetPreview`), but no test covers it. The new e2e test only checks the consumer CSV path. Add a publisher-side check, or at least a unit test confirming that `fetch` receives the `lang` override, so this override bug can't come back unnoticed in either API client.

Skip unsupported records without terminating the ingest. An allosteric-modulator record with action `Neutral` terminates the entire record loop, silently discarding every subsequent interaction. The same problem occurs in the new antagonist, fusion-protein, missing-type, and subunit-specific branches. Use per-record skipping rather than `break` wherever an unsupported combination should be ignored.

Preserve records with missing grouping attributes. Pandas `groupby` defaults to `dropna=True`, so an interaction with a missing `Type`, `Action`, or `Endogenous` is now silently removed during preparation. Previously these records reached the transform, which explicitly supports missing types and actions. Retain null-valued groups and preserve the missing-value representation expected by those branches.

Correct the Agonist spelling in action allowlists. The allowlists contain `Agnoist`, but the source action and the branches below use `Agonist`. Consequently, `Agonist` actions for types `Agonist` and `Allosteric modulator` produce no edges at all, while activators lose their agonism qualifier and additional physical-interaction edge. Correct the spelling in all three lists.

Preserve the inhibition mechanism for fusion proteins. For every fusion-protein interaction with action `Inhibition`, this assignment overwrites the existing `inhibition` mechanism with `molecular_channel_blockage`. Neither the type nor the action establishes channel blockage, and the previous implementation correctly used inhibition. Preserve that mechanism rather than asserting a more specific, unsupported biological mechanism.

`break` here is inside `for record in data:`, so it ends the whole loop. The first Allosteric modulator record with Action 'Neutral' or None stops all further processing, and every record after it is silently dropped from the KG. To skip only this record, use `continue`.
`break` ends the entire record loop. The first Antagonist / 'Partial agonist' record drops every record that follows it. Use `continue`.
`break` ends the entire record loop. The first Fusion protein / 'Binding' record drops every record that follows it. Use `continue`.
`break` ends the entire record loop. The first record with Type None and Action 'Binding' or 'Competitive' drops every record that follows it. Use `continue`.

`break` ends the entire record loop. The first Subunit-specific / 'Mixed' record drops every record that follows it. Use `continue`. The `print` calls should also go: they write to stdout instead of going through `koza.log`.

The list is spelled 'Agnoist' instead of 'Agonist'. Agonist-type records with Action 'Agonist' (the most common agonist case) don't match this branch, and the old fallback branch for Agonist was removed, so these records now produce no edges at all. The `elif record["Action"] == "Agonist"` handler is unreachable.

The 'Agnoist' typo means Activator/Agonist records skip this branch. They fall into the 'not in' branch, where the Agonist mapping was removed. The result is an affects edge with no causal_mechanism_qualifier (agonism is lost) and no directly_physically_interacts_with edge, contrary to the intended mapping.
The 'Agnoist' typo means Allosteric modulator / Agonist records match no branch and are silently dropped. In the old code they produced edges.

`groupby` defaults to `dropna=True`. Any row with a null Type, Action or Endogenous is silently discarded during aggregation. That defeats all the `record["Action"] is None` / `record["Type"] is None` branches and the None entries in the action lists, and loses those interactions entirely. Use `groupby(..., dropna=False)`.

Endogenous is compared case-sensitively to the literal 'TRUE'. GtoPdb CSV booleans are typically lowercase ('true'/'false'). If they are, every record maps to affects/increased/decreased and the regulates/upregulated/downregulated logic never runs. Normalise the value (e.g. `str(...).strip().lower() == 'true'`) and confirm against the real data.

The default predicate is now the string "None" instead of None. Fallback branches that don't set a predicate for an unexpected Action (e.g. Type None or Subunit-specific with another action) will emit an edge with predicate 'None'. That is not a valid Biolink CURIE, so the edge either fails validation or pollutes the graph. Unhandled actions should fail fast or be skipped explicitly.

The old catch-all branches for Antagonist, Antibody, Channel blocker, Fusion protein, Gating inhibitor and Allosteric modulator were replaced with whitelists that have no 'else' path. Any Type/Action combination missing from these lists (or misspelled, as above) is now dropped silently. Nothing logs or counts these dropped records, so data loss after a source update won't be noticed.

Fusion protein / Inhibition now uses `causal_mechanism_qualifier = molecular_channel_blockage`, overriding the `inhibition` value set just above. This looks like a copy-paste from the Channel blocker block. Fusion proteins are not channel blockers, and the earlier assignments in this block are dead code.

For Type None / Action None, a ChemicalAffectsGeneAssociation is built with predicate 'biolink:related_to'. related_to is not a valid predicate for this association class, and the RIG doesn't list it. Use a matching association class/predicate or drop these records. Also note these rows are already removed by the groupby dropna issue.

Aggregation joins raw PubMed ID values without dropping empty strings or deduplicating. An empty value produces an invalid 'PMID:' entry. Because 'Ligand Context' is kept in the earlier drop_duplicates but left out of the grouping, the same PMID can appear more than once on an edge. Filter empties and dedupe, e.g. `'|'.join(sorted(set(...)))`.

Each Type block repeats the same ChemicalAffectsGeneAssociation + PairwiseMolecularInteraction construction, and the `is not None` checks on freshly constructed objects are always true. This copy-paste is how the typo and override bugs above crept in. A declarative (Type, Action) → (mechanism, direction index, emit_physical_edge) mapping table would be far less error-prone and matches the repo's DRY/declarative guidelines. The change also adds no tests for the new mappings.

The RIG node list still declares biolink:Gene for UniProt targets, but the ingest now emits biolink:Protein. The SmallMolecule entry still uses the malformed identifier type 'GTOPDBLigand ID', which this change fixed only for MolecularMixture.

Preserve the literal $schema key in generated headers. PowerShell interpolates `$schema` inside these double-quoted strings. Because that variable is unset, the generated header becomes `# yaml-language-server: =https://...` rather than the required `$schema=...` directive, defeating the manifest-validation fix. Use single-quoted strings or escape the dollar sign in all three schema headers.

The rewritten installer manifest no longer has `PortableCommandAlias: figprint`. The old manifest had it, and the ChangeLog entry for this change says the alias is still set. Without it, WinGet registers the portable command under the exe name (`FIGPrint`) instead of the `figprint` alias that the docs and users expect. Add `    PortableCommandAlias: figprint` under each `NestedInstallerFiles` entry. Line 224 is also a stray blank line inside the array.

This path filter now only matches `FIGLet/**/*.cs`. A release is usually just a version bump in `FIGLet.csproj`, so it will no longer trigger a publish. Changes to embedded fonts/resources and to the workflow file itself are also ignored now. Merging a version-bump PR will silently skip the NuGet release.

This path filter only matches `*.ts`/`*.tsx`. A version bump in `FIGLet.TS/package.json`, changes to `tsconfig`/build config, bundled fonts, or the workflow itself will no longer trigger an npm publish. Release-only PRs will be skipped.
This path filter only matches `FIGLet.Python/**/*.py`. A version bump in `pyproject.toml` or changes to the bundled `.flf` fonts won't trigger a PyPI publish.

This path filter only matches `*.ts`/`*.tsx`. Changes to `FIGLet.VSCodeExtension/package.json` (version bumps, contributed commands/settings like the `defaultFont` removal in this PR), fonts, webpack config, README and CHANGELOG won't trigger a Marketplace publish.
This path filter only matches `*.cs`. Version bumps in `source.extension.vsixmanifest`/`.csproj`, XAML UI changes, and resource changes will no longer trigger a VS Marketplace publish.

The filter now only matches `FIGPrint/**/*.cs` and no longer includes the workflow file. A version bump in `FIGPrint.csproj` won't publish, and the WinGet manifest fixes made to this workflow in this same PR won't run on merge without a manual dispatch.

Behaviour change: the old `editor.selection.isEmpty` / `replace(editor.selection, ...)` branch is gone, so selected text is no longer replaced. The banner is always inserted at column 0 of the cursor line and the selection stays. A user who selects the text to bannerize now ends up with both the banner and the original text. The PR description doesn't mention this, and it is unrelated to the stated fix.

`figlet.defaultFont` is removed with no migration. Users who had set it lose their preference: `lastFontUsed` falls back to `small` until they insert a banner. Seed `lastFontUsed` from the old config value on first run.

The settings panel still shows a selectable font list with `selectedFont` state. Selecting a row is no longer saved and no longer starts from the current font, so the selection is meaningless UI. Either remove the selection affordance or make it clear the list is preview-only.

The new enum member is named `BATCHFile`, which breaks the PascalCase convention of the other members and doesn't match the `BatchFile` property or the ChangeLog wording. CLAUDE.md requires language mappings to stay in sync with `FIGLet.VisualStudioExtension/LanguageCommentStyles.cs`, but the C# side still uses `CommentStyle.Custom` for batch.

The ChangeLog describes the LICENSE ASCII-art banner, but that change was reverted (commit 4e7f43e) and LICENSE isn't in this diff. The revert commit has no entry. The `ci(manifest)` entry also says the `figprint` portable alias is defined, but the manifest no longer contains it. The ChangeLog doesn't match the code being shipped.

Validate flag types before normalizing config-loaded patterns. When a `.techdebtrc.json` custom pattern contains a non-string `flags` value such as `null` or `123`, `validate_config` now throws a TypeError here instead of returning its validation report. `isCustomPatternShape()` checks only required fields, so these values reach `validatePattern()`, and the allowlist check records an error but continues into `.replace()` outside the try block. Check the flag type and skip normalization for invalid values so malformed configuration produces actionable validation errors.

This PR says it guards against ReDoS (#127), but capping pattern length and allowlisting flags doesn't stop catastrophic backtracking. Short patterns like `(a+)+$`, `(.*a){20}` or `(\w|\w)*x` pass `validatePattern` and still run synchronously on every line of up to 500k characters of user input. That blocks the Node event loop and takes the whole MCP server down. Nothing here checks for nested quantifiers (safe-regex / recheck) or bounds execution time (RE2/linear engine, worker thread with timeout, or per-line length cap). The CHANGELOG wording 'preventing ReDoS attacks' overstates the protection, so the issue shouldn't be closed on this change alone.

The new error message `Could not read file stats for: ${path}` puts the raw user-supplied (possibly absolute) path in a response sent to the MCP client. That breaks the project's security rule (#129): use `getRelativePath()` in client-facing errors.

The new size guard runs on a `path` that was never checked with `path.isAbsolute()` or normalized with `path.resolve()` before `fileExists`, `getFileStats` and `readFile`. The CLAUDE.md security rules (#125/#126) require this. Since this block is being hardened anyway, the path should be validated before any filesystem access.

There's a TOCTOU gap between `stat` and `readFile`. The file can grow or be replaced (for example by a symlink swap) after the size check, so `readFile` can still load an unbounded file. Either check the length of the content actually read, or read through a bounded stream or file handle.

The flag-normalization logic (strip, dedupe, default to 'g') is copied verbatim in `executePattern` and `validatePattern` (lines 265-270). Move it into a single private helper so validation and execution can't drift apart. The comment 'Compile with the same normalized flags used at execution time' depends on them staying identical.

`content.split(/\r?\n/)` now runs before the flag normalization and `RegExp` construction. This ordering is harmless, but each rule re-splits up to 500k characters of content. Split the content once in `executeRules` instead, so the work doesn't multiply by the number of rules on the size the PR is trying to bound.

With this change `handlers.ts` grows to about 508 lines. That exceeds the CLAUDE.md limit ('Keep handlers.ts under 500 lines'). The custom-rules handlers should be moved into a dedicated file, as the conventions require.

The capture condition `schema?.method === 'tools/call' || typeof handler === 'function'` is always true, so every handler overwrites `callToolHandler`. The `beforeEach` at 364-365 then relies on the CallTool handler being registered last. The test also adds several `any` types (`callToolHandler: (request: any) => Promise<any>`, `as any`), which the project's no-`any` convention forbids. Capture by schema identity (`schema === CallToolRequestSchema`) and use typed mocks.

The 'accepts at exactly MAX_FILE_SIZE_BYTES' test only checks `.resolves.toBeDefined()`, and `readFile` is mocked so it ignores size. The test would pass even if the boundary comparison were wrong in some other way. It also never asserts that `readFile` is NOT called in the rejection case, which is the actual safety property (the file must not be read into memory).

The README describes the runtime flag stripping/dedup and the pattern-length cap only under `add_custom_rule`. Rules loaded from `.techdebtrc.json` go through `configValidator`, which now rejects bad flags and over-length patterns, so the runtime fallback is effectively for programmatic `addRule` callers only. Also, `validate_custom_pattern` doesn't accept `flags` at all (`handleValidateCustomPattern` drops it), so the 'same validation' claim is only partially true. The docs should say what is actually enforced and where.

Exclude historical volume from the activity check. When a market has zero trades in the last 24 hours but lifetime volume of at least 10, the existing fallback selects `m.volume`, so this new check resets its stale count forever even when price and open interest remain frozen. Such markets also pass the scanner's volume filter, so genuinely inactive markets now bypass staleness filtering. Use recent volume or a positive cumulative-volume delta rather than treating lifetime volume as ongoing activity.

This turns the staleness filter off. `check_staleness` only runs on the output of `filter_markets`, which drops any market where `volume_24h or volume` is below `scanner.min_volume` (default 100, scanner.py:71-73). So every market that reaches this code has volume >= 100, which is above `volume_floor=10`. `has_volume` is therefore always True, every count resets to 0, and nothing is ever skipped. The filter only works when min_volume is set below 10. The expected ~80 candidates is just the full pre-filter list. To catch real inactivity, compare against the previous cycle (e.g. `volume - entry['volume']`, or an OI delta) instead of checking an absolute level.

`volume` is a 24h rolling total, and when `volume_24h` is 0 it falls back to `m.volume`, which is lifetime cumulative volume. Neither measures activity since the last scan cycle. One trade up to 24h ago, or any market whose lifetime volume is >= 10, counts as 'active' forever. Lifetime volume never drops, so a dead market whose 24h volume falls to 0 still passes the floor.

`entry['volume']` is still written every cycle but never read now that the spike comparison is gone. The previous-cycle volume needed to detect new trades is being thrown away. It should be used for a per-cycle delta check, or the field should be removed.

`volume_floor` is hard-coded as a function default. It isn't exposed in ScannerConfig and isn't passed from the CLI, so operators can't tune it or line it up with `min_volume`. That mismatch is what makes the floor meaningless in production.

The tests that check the count increments or reaches the threshold use markets with volume=0 or 9. `filter_markets` (default min_volume=100) would never pass such markets to `check_staleness`. So the tests pass while the production path can never mark anything stale. Add a test that runs filter_markets and then check_staleness with default config, or one that uses volumes at or above min_volume.

The description says markets with 'no volume' are skipped. In practice it's an absolute 24h/lifetime volume floor of 10, below the scanner's own min_volume, so the documented behavior (skipping inactive markets) never happens.

Preserve edits made while synchronization is running. If a user renames an item or edits a comment while a pre-pull/post-push script is running, the final `localRepositoryToProject` replaces the project's entire rename and comment lists with the snapshot captured before the script. Moving synchronization off the EDT now allows those edits, so a successful pull or push silently discards them. Reconcile intervening project changes before applying the result, or prevent editing during synchronization.

Serialize background pull and push operations. Each menu or keyboard invocation now starts an independent thread, so clicking Push twice or starting Pull during Push can concurrently read and overwrite the same repository files and run scripts against the same working copy. `writeRepository` truncates files directly, allowing overlapping operations to lose updates or read partially written JSON. Use a shared operation guard or serialized worker for both actions, covering the final project update as well.

The description says all four entry points go through a shared single-thread daemon executor, but the code doesn't do that. Each menu click or key press starts a new thread with `kotlin.concurrent.thread`, so nothing is queued or serialized. Rapid clicks, or a Pull fired during a Push, will run concurrently. They read and write the same `.local` and remote files (lost updates, torn JSON), run the pre-pull/post-push scripts in parallel, and interleave changes to `codeData`. Before this change, `uiRun` serialized them on the EDT, so this is a regression. Use one shared `Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor` with a daemon thread factory, or guard re-entry with an AtomicBoolean.

`kotlin.concurrent.thread` creates non-daemon threads by default (`isDaemon = false`). The description says a daemon thread prevents a stall at JVM shutdown, but that isn't true here. If a pre-pull or post-push script hangs (`process.waitFor()` has no timeout), or a conflict dialog is pending, these threads will keep the JVM alive after JADX closes.

The project snapshot (`projectToLocalRepository` → `getProjectRenames`/`getProjectComments`) is now taken on a background thread, and the EDT stays responsive while scripts run and conflict dialogs wait for input. At the end, `localRepositoryToProject` on the EDT replaces `codeData.renames`/`comments` completely with the repository contents. Any rename or comment the user makes during the operation isn't in the snapshot, so it is silently thrown away. This couldn't happen before because the EDT was blocked. The same applies to push (lines 589 and 645-648).

`codeData.renames`/`comments` are now read from a background thread and written from the EDT (by the user's own renames and by `localRepositoryToProject`). There is no synchronization or happens-before edge between them, so the background reader can see stale or inconsistent lists. Do the project reads on the EDT (for example with `invokeAndWait`) and keep only the file I/O and scripts in the background.

Nothing on the background thread catches exceptions. `ProcessBuilder.start()` in `runScript` throws IOException for a missing or non-executable script, and `projectToLocalRepository` and the conflict resolver can also throw. Any of these kills the thread and only goes to the default uncaught-exception handler, so the user gets no error dialog and doesn't know the pull or push failed. Wrap the bodies in try/catch and call `showError`.

The tests now call `plugin.pull()`/`push()` directly and no longer run the registered menu or key-binding actions. The captured `pull`/`push` Runnables in PluginMockery are now dead, and nothing tests the new threading or serialization behavior, which is how the missing executor and concurrent runs went unnoticed.

Make audit details available when the LLM judge is disabled. When `LLMJudge.Enabled` is false, `startAdminAPI` does not call `SetEvalRunner`, leaving `a.evalStore` nil. The existing detail handler then rejects this new `getAuditEntry` request with HTTP 503 before reaching `GetEntry`. Since list responses now omit payloads, administrators without an enabled LLM judge can no longer inspect any stored request/response headers or bodies. Remove the eval-store dependency from the audit-detail GET path before relying on it for expansion.

GET /admin/audit now runs an unbounded `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM audit_log` on every page load and every loadMore. With no filters, Postgres has to scan the whole table, so the cost grows with audit history. This works against the PR's goal of lighter list responses, and on a large audit table the count can easily cost more than the 100-row page it describes. If it fails, the whole list returns a 500, where before it still returned entries. Consider counting only on the first page (offset=0), computing has_more by fetching limit+1 rows, or capping or estimating the count.

Fetched details are cached in `entryDetails` by id for the component's lifetime and are never refetched or invalidated. Response bodies are now streamed and written later through UpdateResponse. So if someone expands a row while its request is still in flight, the cached detail shows an empty or partial response body and status, and collapsing and re-expanding keeps showing the stale copy until the page reloads. The cache also keeps every full payload ever expanded in memory. Consider refetching on each expand, or dropping cached details when the list reloads.

While details load, or after the fetch fails, `detailEntry` falls back to the summary row. The expanded panel then shows empty Headers/Body sections next to the 'Loading…' or error message, which looks like the request really had no headers or body. Hide or placeholder the payload sections until the details arrive.

Include diagnostics.js in the published pg-pool package. The `files` allowlist in `packages/pg-pool/package.json` includes only `index.js` and `esm`, so the new `diagnostics.js` module will not be published. Consequently, requiring the published `pg-pool` package (including through `pg`) will fail immediately with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. Add the new module to the package's published files.

Run pool acquisition inside the tracing callback. When instrumentation binds an AsyncLocalStorage store to `pg:pool:connect`'s start channel, that store is active only inside the function passed to `traceCallback`. Here that function merely assigns a callback; the actual acquisition and `client.connect()` happen after the tracing scope has ended. This prevents the new connection trace from inheriting the pool-acquisition context and publishes the synchronous end event before acquisition even starts. Move the acquisition logic into the traced function so downstream connection work runs in the bound context.

index.js now requires './diagnostics', but the `files` field in packages/pg-pool/package.json only lists "index.js" and "esm". The new diagnostics.js will not be in the published tarball, so `require('pg-pool')` (and therefore `pg`'s Pool) will throw 'Cannot find module ./diagnostics' for every user after release. The tests pass only because they run from the source tree. Add diagnostics.js to `files` or inline the module.

The query read-timeout path skips tracing. The readTimeout wrapper captures the original `queryCallback` before traceCallback wraps `query.callback`. When the timer fires, it calls `queryCallback(error)` directly and then overwrites `query.callback = () => {}`, which throws away the traced callback. Queries that hit `query_timeout` therefore emit `start` with no `error` or `asyncEnd`. Spans leak and timeouts are never recorded, even though timeouts are among the most important events to observe. Apply the tracing wrap before the timeout wrapper, or route the timeout through the traced callback.

Queries are traced only when `query.callback` is set. Submittables without a callback (pg-cursor, pg-query-stream, Query objects used through events) are never traced. Errors raised before this point (the `!_queryable` and `_ending` early returns at lines 689-701) also never reach the channel. The PR describes `pg:query` as covering the query lifecycle, so these silent gaps should be closed or documented.

The traced function only assigns `response.callback`. The actual work (newClient → client.connect, pending-queue handling) runs after traceCallback returns, outside the `start.runStores` scope. Any AsyncLocalStorage store a subscriber binds to `pg:pool:connect` is not active while the client connects, so `pg:connection` spans are not parented under the pool-connect span. That defeats much of the point of using TracingChannel instead of plain channels. Run the acquisition logic inside the traced function.

`shouldTrace` returns true when `hasSubscribers` is undefined, so on Node 18.x (where pg's engines `>=16` is still supported) every query, connect and pool.connect goes through traceCallback unconditionally. That adds wrapping overhead even with no subscribers, which contradicts the PR's claim of no overhead. Both test files also skip exactly these versions because of 'internal bugs' in TracingChannel, so the code path that always runs in production on Node 18 is never tested. Either gate on a stable TracingChannel (as the tests do) or test the Node 18 path.

This module duplicates packages/pg/lib/diagnostics.js, including the version-detection logic and the Node 18 `shouldTrace` workaround. The two copies will drift; consider sharing a single implementation or at least keeping them in sync deliberately.

Only the pure-JS Client is instrumented. The native client (packages/pg/lib/native/client.js) emits no `pg:query` or `pg:connection` events, so users of `pg.native` silently lose tracing. Document this or instrument the native client too.

`error: err || undefined` passes through whatever value was given to `release()`. `release(true)` is a common idiom for destroying a client, and it publishes `error: true` instead of an Error. Subscribers recording this as an exception will get a non-Error value; consider normalizing it or documenting it.

The outer `testTracing('query diagnostics channel', function () { testTracing(...) })` nests test registrations inside a test body. With this repo's simple Suite helper, the outer 'test' takes no `done` and registers inner tests while it is running, so the inner tests may not run or report as intended. Also, assertion failures inside subscriber callbacks will throw out of `publish` into pg's code instead of failing the test cleanly. Verify that these tests actually run and fail when they should.

Flush pending changes before switching workspaces. If a workspace is switched or created within 300 ms of an edit, this cleanup cancels the outgoing workspace's pending save. Neither switch handler flushes the current state first, so those edits are permanently lost when returning to the workspace. Persist the outgoing data before replacing it, rather than simply cancelling its timer.

Implement the presigning bridge required by S3 sync. Every S3 push and pull calls `electronAPI.getPresignedUrl`, but the updated preload exposes no such method and the main process registers no corresponding handler. Consequently S3 sync always throws the Electron-required error even inside Electron. Implement the IPC method and signing handler before exposing this provider.

Encrypt credentials before persisting sync configuration. Saving any provider configuration writes its tokens, passwords, or AWS secrets directly into `sync-config.json` and localStorage, including in Electron. The encryption helpers are never invoked, so the advertised encrypted credential storage does not exist. Encrypt secret fields before both persistence writes and decrypt them when loading configuration for use.

Track the last successful sync for conflict detection. The configuration passed to `syncPull` never contains `lastSynced`, and successful pushes and pulls never persist that timestamp. Since the engine requires both remote and local timestamps before throwing `ConflictError`, the conflict banner is unreachable and pulls silently overwrite local changes even after previous syncs. Persist the sync timestamp and include it in subsequent operations.

Retry pushing existing commits when the working tree is clean. If a push fails after the commit succeeds, for example because of invalid credentials or a network outage, retrying with unchanged workspace data returns success here without executing `git.push`. The outstanding commit therefore never reaches the remote despite the UI reporting success. Skip only the commit for a clean working tree, not the push.

Delete snapshot files when pruning the history index. After 50 saves, slicing the index removes old entries but leaves their full workspace snapshot files on disk forever. Because each debounced save creates another complete copy, storage consumption grows without bound while the orphaned snapshots cannot even be accessed from History. Delete the files belonging to entries removed from the index.

The description says this change adds `jsonwebtoken` and `bcryptjs` as runtime dependencies, but package.json only gains `simple-git`. package-lock.json lists `bcryptjs` and `jsonwebtoken` as root dependencies, so the manifest and lockfile disagree and `npm ci` fails with 'lock file out of sync'. Also, nothing in the repo requires these packages: there is no `server/team/` directory, and the README says the team server moved to a separate project. Either drop them from the lockfile or add them to package.json, and fix the description.

The git sync routes take `dataDir` from the request body. The server uses `cors()` with every origin allowed. So any web page the user visits can POST to localhost and make the server create directories, run `git init`, write `workspace.json` under any path it picks, change git config there, and fetch from or push to an attacker-chosen remote. Use only `process.env.APILIX_DATA_DIR` on the server, and restrict CORS or add an auth token for these routes.

Push returns 'Nothing to commit' and skips `git push` whenever the working tree is clean. If an earlier push committed locally but failed on the network or auth step, every later Push reports success and the commit never reaches the remote. Push regardless of whether there is something new to commit.

The username and token are written into the remote URL passed to git. Git error messages often contain that URL, and `err.message` is sent back to the renderer unchanged, which can expose the token in the UI. `new URL(remote)` also throws on SSH-style remotes (`git@host:repo`) whenever a username and token are filled in. Pass credentials through a credential helper or an http.extraHeader, and strip secrets from error text.

S3 sync cannot work. The adapter reads `config.keyId` and `config.secret`, but the UI saves `accessKeyId` and `secretAccessKey`, so the credentials are always undefined. `window.electronAPI.getPresignedUrl` is also never exposed in preload.js, and main.js has no IPC handler for it, so every S3 push or pull throws 'requires Electron' even inside Electron.

Sync credentials are stored in plaintext. `writeSyncConfig` never calls `encryptValue`: Git tokens, AWS secret keys and JWTs go unencrypted into sync-config.json and are also copied into localStorage even in Electron. This contradicts the docs ('stored encrypted', safeStorage) and the comment in types.ts. Encrypt the secret fields before writing and don't mirror secrets to localStorage.

Conflict detection never runs. Nothing ever sets `lastSynced`: the UI builds SyncConfig without it, and `writeSyncConfig` doesn't save it. So `localTs` is always null and every Pull silently overwrites local data. Even when set, the timestamps are compared as raw strings. HTTP and S3 return RFC 1123 dates (`Mon, 01 Jan ...`) and git returns ISO with an offset, so lexical comparison against an ISO string gives wrong answers. Parse both into Date objects before comparing.

With 'keep-local', `pull` returns null and the comment says 'caller will push instead', but the caller in WorkspaceManagerModal doesn't push. It shows 'Remote is empty — nothing to pull', which is misleading, and the conflict is never resolved.

The cleanup function cancels pending debounced saves when the workspace changes. Switching, creating or duplicating a workspace within 300 ms of an edit clears the timer for the old workspace, and the new effect writes only the new workspace, so the last edits to the previous workspace are lost. Flush the pending save before switching, or capture the workspace id and data at schedule time and don't cancel on workspace change.

Every debounced save (300 ms, not the 1–2 s the docs say) also creates a full workspace snapshot. That includes no-op saves right after hydrate or switch. Snapshots get written for every burst of edits, and the 50-entry history fills with near-identical copies within minutes, so useful restore points get pushed out. Throttle snapshots and skip them when nothing changed.

The tab session is no longer saved or restored. The old code saved `tabSession` and reopened open tabs and the active tab on launch; the new code drops both, and the migration ignores `legacy.tabSession`. Users lose their open tabs on every restart. That's a regression not mentioned in the description.

`init()` has no error handling. If `writeManifest` or `writeWorkspace` rejects (for example an IPC write error, or `assertInsideUserData` throwing), `HYDRATE_WORKSPACE` is never dispatched and the app is stuck on the 'Loading…' screen with no recovery. Wrap it in try/catch and fall back to an empty Default workspace.

The 'ring buffer' only trims the index. Snapshot files that drop out of the 50-entry index are never deleted, so `snapshots/` grows without limit. Combined with a full-workspace snapshot on every save, disk use grows quickly. Delete the snapshot files that fall off the index.

Pull and Import replace collections through `HYDRATE_WORKSPACE`, which doesn't reset `tabs`, `activeTabId` or `activeRequest`. Open tabs keep pointing at items from the old collections and can write stale data back on save.
Push and Duplicate read workspace data from disk, not from in-memory state. Edits made in the last 300 ms, before the debounced save, aren't included in what gets pushed or copied.

Clicking any provider button clears every field, including the saved config loaded for the current provider. Clicking the already-selected provider by accident wipes the user's credentials from the form.

Duplicating a workspace copies `type`, `role`, `teamServerUrl` and `teamServerId` from the source. A copy of a team workspace still shows as a team workspace even though it has no sync config or server binding.

Pressing Enter calls `commitRename`, and the input then unmounts and fires `onBlur`, which calls `commitRename` again. The result is a duplicate dispatch and a second manifest write built from a stale `state.workspaces`.
Dead code: `manageOpen` is never set to true because nothing in ActivityBar calls `setManageOpen(true)`, so this modal never renders. Remove it or add a trigger button.

Light mode remaps `.bg-purple-700` globally to a pale purple to fix one websocket toggle. Every other element using `bg-purple-700` with white text becomes low-contrast in light mode. Scope the selector to that toggle.

Track successful checkpoint loading explicitly. When a checkpoint exists but loading fails (for example, because its architecture is incompatible), the pipeline initializes a replacement model and assigns a new `q`. This condition then incorrectly marks that model as loaded and skips training, silently producing results from untrained weights. Set the loaded flag from the actual outcome of `load_model`, before initializing any replacement.

Preserve the grid-search plotting file contract. After a grid-search run, `plot_encoding_dim` still reads `grid_search.csv` with columns `encod_dim` and `aucpr`, but this writer now emits `grid_search_results.csv` with different column names. Consequently, the documented encoding-dimension plotting command fails with `FileNotFoundError` on fresh output. Update the reader alongside the writer or retain the existing file contract.

Restore centering metadata for non-PCA checkpoints. With `init_pca=False`, training constructs the encoder with protein means and no encoder bias, whereas loading always constructs it with `prot_means=None` and an encoder bias. Its state dictionary therefore cannot load, and the means used to center inputs are not saved either. Persist and restore the centering mode and means so checkpoints from this supported configuration can actually be reused.

Refit location and scale when replacing fitted degrees of freedom. When `common_degrees_freedom=False` and a protein's fitted degrees of freedom are below 3 or rejected as non-converged, this branch replaces them but retains location and scale estimated for the original distribution. P-values are then calculated using a distribution that was never fitted to the residuals, compromising outlier calibration. Refit location and scale with the replacement degrees of freedom, as the common-DF branch does.

This change does not make checkpointing opt-in, though the description says it does. When `checkpoint_path` is unset, the code falls back to `out_dir/model.pt` and `checkpoint_path` is always truthy. So every run still writes a checkpoint, and every later run with the same `out_dir` silently loads it and skips latent-dim search and training. Commenting the key out of config.yaml has no effect on this. If the goal is opt-in, skip save and load when `config.checkpoint_path` is None.

A loaded checkpoint is never checked against the current run. Only the shape of the state_dict has to match. It does not store or compare the protein IDs and their order, the sample/covariate setup, init_pca, h_dim, log_func or the find_q_method. If a user reruns with new data that has the same number of proteins, or with changed hyperparameters, into the same out_dir, the old model is reused and the outlier calls are silently wrong. Store a fingerprint of the protein index and the relevant config in the checkpoint and refuse to load on a mismatch.

`load_model` always rebuilds the model with `prot_means=None`. A model trained with `init_pca=False` is built with prot_means: its encoder has no bias and it subtracts the means in forward. Loading that checkpoint fails on missing/unexpected keys, the broad `except` hides the error, and the model is retrained on every run. Because prot_means is not saved in the state_dict, even a load that succeeded would run the forward pass without centering.

`torch.load(..., weights_only=False)` unpickles arbitrary objects, so a crafted .pt file can execute code. The file is loaded automatically from out_dir or a user-supplied path. The checkpoint only holds tensors and primitives, so use `weights_only=True`.
Any exception while loading becomes a warning and a silent retrain, and the retrain then overwrites the checkpoint. Real errors such as a corrupt file or a device problem are hidden from the user.

In `train_and_eval_q`, the non-finite-loss branch assigns `auc_prec_rec = np.nan`, but the function returns `auprc`. Any diverged fit during grid or binary search raises UnboundLocalError and the whole run crashes. Assign `auprc = np.nan` instead.

`max(enc2auprc, key=enc2auprc.get)` behaves unpredictably when some AUPRC values are NaN, because NaN comparisons are always False. The result depends on iteration order and can pick a NaN entry. Filter out NaN values first, or use `np.nanargmax`.

The binary search starts with `R = int(q * 3)` and never bounds it. `k_max` is computed but never used, so R (and later midpoints) can go past the number of proteins or samples. That leads to invalid latent dims, or PCA init with a Vt_q that is too large. Clamp R to `min(k_max, n_samples - 1)`.

The binary-search loop has logic bugs. (1) After the 'shrink' branch runs, control falls through into the 'shift' `if fR > fM / else` in the same iteration, which moves M using the newly evaluated L/R. An `elif`/`continue` is missing. (2) `best_q/best_f` is only updated at the top of each iteration, so points evaluated in the last iteration are never considered. (3) The loop variable `q` shadows the OHT `q`. The search can return a sub-optimal latent dim.
`perform_svd()` and OHT now run unconditionally, even when the user gives a fixed integer q. For 'gs' they run a second time at line 92. This adds a full SVD of extra cost to every run.
A leftover debug `print(data_shape)` is in library code. Remove it, or use logger.debug.

Grid-search results are now written to `grid_search_results.csv` with columns `enc_dim`/`auprc`. The old `grid_search.csv` (`encod_dim`/`aucpr`) is no longer written. `plot_encoding_dim` still reads `grid_search.csv` and the old column names, so `protrider plot encoding_dim` (and `all`) fails with FileNotFoundError or KeyError.

`find_latent_dim` always returns a GridSearchResult, so `gs_results is not None` is always true on a fresh run. For OHT or a fixed q this writes an empty grid_search_results.csv. When a checkpoint is loaded, gs_result is None and no file is written, so output files differ between identical configs depending on whether a checkpoint exists.

config.yaml sets `common_degrees_freedom: False`, but the dataclass default in config.py is `True` and both comments say common df is 'more stable for small datasets'. The template therefore enables the less stable per-protein df path by default, and CLI and Python-API users get different p-values from the same settings.

In the `use_common_df=False` branch, the fallback `df0` is recomputed inside the loop from the partly filled `df` array. Early proteins always fall back to 10, and later ones use a median of whatever was filled so far, including earlier fallback values. The p-values for non-converged proteins then depend on column order. Compute df0 once from all first-pass dfs before the loop.
The common-df path now clamps the median df to at least 3 (`max(df0, 3.0)`). This is an unannounced change to p-values for existing users, and the PR describes nothing beyond two small fixes.

`train` now adds ReduceLROnPlateau and early stopping on the training loss, then restores the best weights. It also still returns the last epoch's `running_loss`, which no longer matches the restored model. Together with the ReLU→GELU switch and the newly added biases in multi-layer models, this changes model results for all users without being mentioned in the PR. The description claims only two one-line fixes, but the diff includes CV removal, checkpointing, wandb, binary search, per-protein df and a public `run()` return-signature change (2-tuple → 4-tuple, which breaks API callers). It should be split up or described properly so these changes can be reviewed.

For n_layers > 1, PCA init now writes PCA weights into only the first encoder layer and the last decoder layer. The GELU and the randomly initialized middle layers sit in between, so the 'PCA initialization' no longer approximates a PCA reconstruction, yet it is applied without any warning.

Compare reviewed commit identity instead of commit timestamps. If an existing commit is pushed after Copilot submits its review, its committer date can still precede the review. This comparison then marks unreviewed changes as fresh and prevents requesting another review. Commit timestamps do not establish which revision was reviewed; compare the review's `commit_id` with the PR's current head SHA instead.

Account for pagination when determining review freshness. Both collection requests retrieve only the first page (30 entries by default). For a PR with more than 30 commits, this treats commit 30 as the latest and can skip a required review of subsequent commits. For more than 30 reviews, it can miss the latest Copilot review and request a duplicate. Follow pagination for reviews and retrieve the actual PR head rather than taking the last commit on the first page.

Check freshness before minimizing the existing review. When the existing review is fresh, `run` has already called `MinimizeCopilotComments`, which hides all Copilot review overviews as outdated. This new early return then leaves the current review hidden without requesting a replacement. Perform the freshness check before minimizing reviews so a no-op invocation preserves the up-to-date review.

Freshness is decided by comparing the last commit's committer date with the review's submitted_at. The committer date is set on the author's machine when the commit is created, not when it is pushed. A commit created before Copilot's review but pushed (or force-pushed/rebased with preserved dates) after it will make the review look fresh, so the tool skips a review that is actually needed. Clock skew can cause the same problem. The PR description says the check compares each review's `commit_id` with the PR head SHA, which is the reliable approach, but the code doesn't do that. Fetch `head.sha` from the PR and compare it with the Copilot reviews' `commit_id`.

`pulls/{n}/commits` is paginated and returns 30 commits by default. `c.rest.Get` only reads the first page. On PRs with more than 30 commits, `commits[len(commits)-1]` is the 30th commit, not the head, so an old date is compared and a stale review can be treated as fresh. The PR description says `--paginate` is used, but it isn't. Use the PR's `head.sha` (or `head` commit) instead of listing commits.

The reviews list is also paginated (30 per page) and only the first page is read. On PRs with many reviews, Copilot's latest review may be on a later page, so the tool either misses it (and asks for an unneeded review) or uses an older one. `HasCopilotPendingReview` has the same problem.

`MinimizeCopilotComments` runs unconditionally before the new freshness check and minimizes every Copilot review as OUTDATED, including the one that is current. When the review turns out to be fresh, the command prints "already up to date" and returns. By then the up-to-date review has already been hidden as outdated and no new review is requested, so the PR ends up with no visible current Copilot review. Run the freshness check before minimizing, or skip minimizing when the review is fresh.

The implementation doesn't match the PR description. The description promises a `CheckCopilotReviewStatus()` method that combines the pending and fresh checks into one API call, a `commit_id` vs head SHA comparison, and `gh api --paginate --jq` with `json.Decoder`. Instead, the code adds a separate `IsCopilotReviewFresh` that compares timestamps, keeps `HasCopilotPendingReview`, and doesn't paginate. Reviewers and the test plan are working from behaviour the code doesn't have.

The reviews endpoint is now fetched twice, once in `HasCopilotPendingReview` and again in `IsCopilotReviewFresh`, plus an extra commits request. This uses more rate limit, which the description says the change was meant to avoid. Fetch the reviews once and work out both pending and fresh status from that single response.

Every Copilot review counts toward the latest time regardless of state, including DISMISSED reviews. A dismissed review submitted after the last commit makes the tool skip asking for a new review. Consider filtering by state.

Dispatch layer actions through the atom action API. When any overlay is mounted during a basemap switch, these calls do not dispatch its disable/enable actions: `LayerAtom` is a Reatom atom, not a function accepting action names. Use its action creators and dispatch them (for example, `layer.disable.dispatch()`). Otherwise the callback fails and overlays removed by the style replacement are never restored. The test hides this problem by substituting a callable `vi.fn()` for a real layer atom.

Wait for the replacement style to load before restoring overlays. When `setStyle` diffs against an existing style, `styledata` can fire synchronously before this listener is registered, or fire while the replacement style is not yet fully loaded. Consequently restoration can be skipped or attempted before sources can safely be added. Register the completion listener before calling `setStyle` and use the style-load completion event rather than the first `styledata` notification.

Calling `layer('disable')` and `layer('enable')` does not dispatch anything. `mountedLayersAtom` holds reatom v2 logical layer atoms, and calling a v2 atom as a function runs its internal `(transaction, cache)` reducer. A plain string is not a valid transaction, so this will likely throw inside the `styledata` handler or silently do nothing. The codebase dispatches these actions as `dispatch(layer.enable())` (see src/features/mcda/atoms/mcdaLayer.ts:100), e.g. `store.dispatch([layer.disable(), layer.enable()])`. The unit test hides this because it stores a `vi.fn()` in the atom. In the real app the existing layers are wiped by `setStyle` and never come back.

Even with correct dispatch, running disable and then enable back to back is unlikely to remount anything. The logical layer reducer only calls `willUnMount`/`willMount` when `isEnabled !== isMounted` after a state update, and it skips the sync step on the same pass where `isMounted` changes. A synchronous disable followed by enable can end with `isEnabled` and `isMounted` both true, so `willMount` never runs. Also, `enable` pushes `getMutualExcludedActions`, which can turn off other layers as a side effect. A dedicated remount path is needed: reset each renderer's `_layerIds`/`_sourceId` and call `renderer.willMount`.

`willUnMount` was not updated for the style-URL case. Disabling the Kontur basemap layer leaves its style on the map, and the default `configRepo.get().mapBaseStyle` is never restored. So the basemap can be switched on but never switched back off, which defeats the goal of 'basemap switching'. Restore the default style on unmount, and remount the other layers there too.

`_updateMap` is shared by `willMount`, `willSourceUpdate` and `willLegendUpdate`. Any later source or legend update for the basemap layer (for example a deep-frozen source object being replaced) will call `setStyle` again and tear down and remount every layer on the map. Only call `setStyle` when the style URL actually changes, e.g. by storing the current style URL on the renderer.

Each call to `layersOrderManager.init` pushes another `layersSettingsAtom.subscribe` onto `_unsubscribe` without removing the old one. Every basemap switch therefore leaks a subscription. Either make `init` idempotent by unsubscribing first, or add a dedicated method that only recomputes `_baseMapFirstLayerIdx` after a style change.

`styledata` fires for many style mutations, not only for a finished style load. A `styledata` from some other change (for example a layer mutation still in flight) can trigger the remount before the new style has finished loading. The remount would then run against the old or partially loaded style and compute a wrong `_baseMapFirstLayerIdx`. Use `style.load`, or check `map.isStyleLoaded()` inside the handler. Also, nothing handles a failed style load (`error` event), so the user gets no feedback when that happens.

Other renderers keep stale internal state after `setStyle` (`_layerIds`, `_sourceId`, cached click listeners). Their `willUnMount` will log 'Layer doesn't exist' warnings for layers that `setStyle` already removed. `GenericRenderer.mountTileLayer`/`mountGeoJSONLayer` may also early-return based on stale state. Clearing `mapLibreParentsIds` globally also drops parent mappings the layers need. Consider passing `{ diff: false }`, and make remounting a deliberate renderer-level operation.

For the style-URL branch, `this._layerIds` stays empty, so the `if (!isVisible) this.willHide({ map })` that follows is a silent no-op. Hiding the basemap layer does nothing. A missing `urls[0]` is also skipped silently. Add a warning or error so developers learn the source is malformed.

The test cannot catch the real dispatch bug. It stores a `vi.fn()` in `mountedLayersAtom` instead of a real logical layer atom, so it checks a calling convention that does not work in production. It also only checks that 'disable' was called, not 'enable', and never checks that `layersOrderManager.init` ran. The assertion messages also lack input context, which AGENTS.md asks for. Use a real `createLogicalLayerAtom` with a stub renderer and assert that `willMount` is called again.
`{ virtual: true }` is a Jest option. Vitest's `vi.mock` does not support it, so the argument is ignored and misleading.

`initSpy.mockRestore()` runs only after the assertions pass. If an assertion fails, `layersOrderManager.init` stays mocked for the rest of the test file. Restore it in `afterEach`, or use `vi.restoreAllMocks`.

Reject resolved paths outside the root before parent fallback. If a file inside the storage root is a symlink to an external file, canonicalizing it succeeds but fails the containment check; execution then falls through and accepts its in-root parent. Consequently, `write_file` can truncate the external target and `harden_file` can change its permissions, defeating the new containment guarantee. Return an error when successful full-path canonicalization resolves outside the root, and reserve the parent fallback for genuinely nonexistent files.

`validate_path` can be bypassed with a symlink. If the target is a symlink inside the storage root that points outside it, the first check fails because the canonical path is outside the root. The code then falls through to the parent check, which passes because the link sits inside the root. The parent fallback should only run when the path does not exist; existing paths that resolve outside the root should be rejected. As written, `write_file` and `harden_file` follow the link and write to or chmod a file outside the root, which this change is meant to prevent.

`write_file` opens with `create+truncate` but without `O_NOFOLLOW`, then calls `set_permissions` on the path, which also follows symlinks. Combined with the `validate_path` fallback, a pre-planted symlink makes this truncate, overwrite and chmod an arbitrary file the daemon can write. Even with validation fixed, there is a TOCTOU window between the check and the open. Use `custom_flags(libc::O_NOFOLLOW)` and `file.set_permissions(...)` on the open handle instead of the path.

`harden_file` calls `std::fs::set_permissions(path)`, which follows symlinks. Because of the `validate_path` fallback, a symlink at the allocated path gets its target chmod'ed even if the target is outside the root. Check `symlink_metadata` and refuse non-regular files, the way `move_file` already does.

The 'file-first' ordering is not crash-safe as claimed. If `delete_file` fails (e.g. `validate_path` rejects a row whose path is outside the current root because base_dir moved or the row is legacy, or a permission error), the error is only logged and the DB row is deleted anyway. The file then stays on disk with no record, so retention silently fails to remove user media. For paths outside the media subdirs, the orphan sweep will never find it either. Keep the row (or count the failure) when file deletion fails with anything other than NotFound.

Files are now removed before their DB rows are deleted, in a separate non-transactional step. During that window, readers (search results, OCR loop, IPC clients) can get rows whose media no longer exists. The comment says such orphan rows are 'easy to detect', but no code detects or repairs DB rows pointing to missing files.

Only `chronicle.db` is chmod'ed to 0o600. The `-wal` and `-shm` sidecars, which hold recent unencrypted data, keep their umask-derived mode. The DB is also created by SQLite before the chmod. Existing `screenshots/`/`audio/` subdirectories and files from earlier installs are never re-hardened, because `DirBuilder::mode` only applies to newly created directories. The base dir at 0o700 currently mitigates this, but the 0o600 claim in the summary is incomplete.

`set_permissions(&base_dir, 0o700)` follows symlinks and runs unconditionally on every open. If base_dir is a symlink or a user-supplied shared directory, this silently changes permissions on the target. Consider checking `symlink_metadata` first, or only hardening directories this code creates.

`move_file` is a public API that accepts any `from` path without validation. Any caller can move arbitrary files (e.g. from elsewhere in the user's home) into the storage root and then delete them. If the source must be the staging dir, validate it against an allowed staging root.

`dummy_media_mgr` uses a fixed, shared, world-writable `/tmp/chronicle-test-dummy` instead of a tempdir. Tests are not hermetic and leave state behind across runs and users; another user who owns that path first makes the tests fail. Use `tempfile::tempdir()`.

`files.rs` is now entirely `#[cfg(test)]` dead code. It keeps duplicate copies of `sanitize_id`/`date_parts` that production no longer uses, so its tests check code that is not the code shipped in `media.rs`. Delete the module, or move these tests to `media.rs`.

The change now passes `cancellationToken` to `SendPingAsync`, but `PingDeviceAsync` has no catch for `OperationCanceledException`, so the generic `catch (Exception)` handles it. On shutdown or any cancellation, every in-flight ping logs a spurious 'Unexpected error pinging' warning (one per device, since all devices are checked in parallel) and returns `false`. `CheckDeviceAsync` then treats that as the device going offline: it sets `IsOnline = false` and `OnlineSince = null` and tries to persist and broadcast the change, which can wrongly flip online devices to offline during shutdown. Add `catch (OperationCanceledException) when (cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested) { throw; }` (or a plain rethrow) before the generic catch so cancellation reaches `ExecuteAsync`, which already handles it.

The iputils-ping hint is in the wrong catch block. On Linux, when .NET cannot open a raw socket it falls back to running the `ping` binary, and if that binary is missing it throws `PlatformNotSupportedException` ('ping utility not found'), not `PingException`. So the 'install iputils-ping / CAP_NET_RAW' guidance belongs in the `PlatformNotSupportedException` warning, which currently logs only a generic message, and only once. The `PingException` path logs the hint at Debug level on every failure, where operators are unlikely to see it. Move the hint into the once-only warning.
