Once ping is unsupported, every device is reported offline on every cycle, and the only signal is a single warning logged for the whole service lifetime. That warning is easy to miss, and nothing in the device status shows that offline means 'could not check' rather than 'unreachable'. Consider logging at Error level, or exposing the condition, for example by disabling monitoring or surfacing it through `IDeviceMonitoringService`.

The using cleanup also adds a UTF-8 BOM (`\uFEFF`) at the start of the file. This creates an unrelated encoding change that adds noise to the diff and may clash with the repo's encoding conventions. Remove it.

Qualify the Codex instruction references with their install directory. When Codex runs from a project directory, these bare `@...` references do not identify the files installed in `~/.codex/`. Unlike Claude's import syntax, they do not automatically include those files, so the shared rules and personas can remain unread or resolve to project files instead. Explicitly direct Codex to read the files under its configuration directory.

Make correction persistence specific to the active tool. Installing this skill into Codex and Gemini now directs those tools to persist cross-project corrections in `~/.claude/AGENTS.md` and context in Claude's memory directory. Consequently, corrections do not reach the active tool's future sessions and can unexpectedly modify another tool's configuration. Parameterize these destinations or keep this implementation Claude-specific, consistent with the tool-specific separation described in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#L7).

Codex CLI can't import files with `@file`. It loads ~/.codex/AGENTS.md as plain text, so `@INSTRUCTIONS.md`, `@AGENT-PERSONA.md`, `@USER-PERSONA.md` and `@CODEX-EXTENSIONS.md` are never expanded. At best the model has to decide on its own to read them, and a bare relative name would be looked up in the project's working directory, not ~/.codex/. In practice Codex users lose all the laws, constraints, workflow and persona content this PR moved out of the instruction file. For Codex, inline the content into AGENTS.md at install time, or use absolute ~/.codex/ paths with an explicit instruction to read them.

The core laws, constraints and workflow used to be inline. Now they are only loaded if Claude Code resolves `@INSTRUCTIONS.md` and `@CLAUDE-EXTENSIONS.md` written mid-sentence, two levels of imports deep (CLAUDE.md → AGENTS.md → INSTRUCTIONS.md). The test plan says this is unverified. The persona imports also changed from standalone `@` lines to inline prose. Confirm that the imports resolve, or put each `@` reference on its own line as before, before merging. If they don't resolve, every Claude session silently loses its core instructions.

CLAUDE-EXTENSIONS.md imports `@INSTRUCTIONS.md` again, but AGENTS.md already imports it. That can load the shared instructions into context twice. Mention the file by name instead of `@`-importing it.

This content is described as tool-agnostic and gets installed into Codex and Gemini, but it relies on Claude-only features: Claude Code's plan mode, beads ("bead"), and the superpowers-plugin skills `verification-before-completion` and `self-improving-agent`, plus `context7`. Other tools will be told to use skills and modes that don't exist for them. Move these references into CLAUDE-EXTENSIONS.md or word them generically.

The PR presents this as a pure extraction, but the 'Decide, don't defer' rule was reworded and broadened. It used to apply only 'when presenting plans or designs for review'. It now applies everywhere and adds 'Don't ask clarifying questions for decisions you can reasonably make yourself.' This changes agent behaviour without being mentioned in the PR description. Split it into its own change or call it out.

Agent files are copied into ~/.gemini/agents (and ~/.codex/agents) unchanged. Their frontmatter is Claude-specific: `model: sonnet|opus|haiku|inherit` and a `color` field. Gemini CLI subagents expect Gemini model names and their own schema, so these definitions may fail to load or be rejected, despite the PR claiming Gemini uses them 'natively'. Translate or filter the frontmatter for each tool, or skip agents for tools whose format isn't confirmed compatible.

Shared and tool-specific content now go into the same destination folders (skills/, agents/), but the 'exists in dest but not in source' warning only checks the source being synced. Once a tool-specific skills/ or agents/ directory exists, every shared item will be reported as 'not in <tool>-specific source', and every tool-specific item as 'not in shared source', on every run. Check against both sources before warning.

If a shared item and a tool-specific item have the same name (for example in skills/), Phase 2 installs the shared one and Phase 5 then sees a difference and offers to replace it. On the next run Phase 2 sees a difference again, so the two keep overwriting each other and the user is prompted on every run. Skip the shared item when a tool-specific override with the same name exists.

Auto-detect always includes claude, even if ~/.claude doesn't exist, and creates the directory. Codex and Gemini are only detected if their directory exists. This is inconsistent, and on a machine with only Codex or Gemini it will create an unwanted ~/.claude.

Reject callbacks for already-completed sessions. If two successful GitHub authorization callbacks use the same state before token redemption, this code generates two internal codes pointing to the same mutable session. The second callback overwrites the access token associated with the first code, and redeeming either code leaves the other redeemable even after the session is deleted. Reject completion when the session already has an internal code so that a completed authorization cannot change identity or produce multiple redeemable grants.

PKCE is optional. If `code_challenge` is missing, /authorize accepts the request, and ExchangeCode (session.go:111-115) skips verification entirely. Anyone who intercepts the internal code (for example, another local process listening on a localhost port, or through logs or history) can redeem it for the user's GitHub token. OAuth 2.1 and the MCP auth spec require PKCE for public clients, so /authorize should reject requests that lack `code_challenge`.

Sessions are keyed only by the `state` value the client supplies, and SaveSession overwrites any existing entry without checking. A second /authorize with the same state (an attacker who saw the state in the GitHub URL, or two clients using the same simple state) replaces the redirect_uri and code_challenge of a flow already in progress. The victim's callback then issues a code bound to the attacker's challenge and redirect. Generate an internal state server-side for the GitHub leg, or refuse to overwrite an existing state.

CompleteCallback does not consume or mark the session. Calling /callback again with the same state (and another GitHub code) mints another internal code on the same *Session and overwrites AccessToken, Scope and InternalCode in place. Earlier codes stay in `s.codes` and point to the mutated session, so an old code can redeem a newer token. ExchangeCode also deletes only the presented code, leaving the others redeemable. A session should complete only once.

Callback reads the session through lookupByCode after CompleteCallback has released the lock, then uses `sess.RedirectURI` without synchronization. A concurrent /token or a second /callback can delete or mutate the same session in between, causing spurious 'session lost' errors or a data race. CompleteCallback should return the redirect_uri atomically along with the code.

/authorize is unauthenticated and stores a session for every request, keyed by an arbitrary-length client state. Nothing limits the number of sessions or the size of the state. A burst of requests can grow memory without bound until the janitor runs after the TTL, and the container has a 256M memory limit. Cap the state length, cap the number of pending sessions, or rate-limit the endpoint.

ValidateToken accepts any token that GitHub's /user endpoint accepts: any PAT, or any OAuth token from any app and any user. It does not check that the token was issued by this façade or has the expected audience or client. The MCP auth spec forbids this kind of token passthrough without an audience check, and the server is then reachable by any GitHub user. At minimum, restrict access to allowed logins, or issue façade-owned tokens.

Only status codes 5xx are treated as upstream errors. GitHub rate limiting returns 403 or 429, and those are reported to the client as 401 invalid_token. Clients will then drop valid tokens and restart the OAuth flow during a rate-limit window. Treat 403/429 with rate-limit headers as upstream errors (503).

The discovery metadata omits `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported`. Under RFC 8414 the default is `client_secret_basic`, so compliant clients will assume they must authenticate with a client secret they don't have. It also omits `registration_endpoint`, so MCP clients cannot obtain a client_id. Advertise `["none"]`.

When the user denies consent, GitHub redirects to /callback with `error=access_denied` and no code. That case returns a plain-text 400 'missing code or state' instead of redirecting the error and state back to the client's redirect_uri (RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1), so the MCP client never learns that the flow failed.

BASE_URL defaults to http://localhost:8083 regardless of COPILOT_REVIEW_MCP_PORT. If the port is changed, the discovery metadata and the GitHub callback URL point to the wrong port and the OAuth flow breaks. Derive the default from the same variable, e.g. `http://localhost:${COPILOT_REVIEW_MCP_PORT:-8083}`.

SESSION_TTL_MIN and TOKEN_CACHE_TTL_MIN are not validated. Zero or negative values are accepted silently, so every session expires immediately and the OAuth flow always fails with 'invalid state'. Reject non-positive values or fall back to the default.
The placeholder MCP handler only registers `GET /mcp`. MCP Streamable HTTP clients send JSON-RPC over `POST /mcp`, so an authenticated client gets a 405 and the end-to-end flow cannot be exercised.

Preserve syntax compatibility with supported Ruby versions. The safe-navigation operator requires Ruby 2.3, but README.md and fastimage.gemspec still support Ruby 1.9.2 and later. On Ruby 1.9–2.2, requiring fastimage now raises SyntaxError, breaking all existing functionality, not just resolution extraction. The new keyword-argument syntax in Exif also excludes Ruby 1.9. Use syntax compatible with the declared minimum version.

Read resolution rationals at valid backward offsets. TIFF offsets may point to rational data before the IFD, and XResolution and YResolution may share the same rational value offset. Skipping every offset behind the current stream position silently loses resolution in both valid layouts: data before the IFD is never read, and a shared offset is skipped after reading the first axis. Consequently, the public API returns nil despite available resolution metadata. Preserve referenced bytes or support seeking and reuse values for shared offsets.

A truncated or malformed JFIF APP0 segment crashes the call. The only check is that the first 5 bytes are "JFIF\0", then `data[7].ord` and `data[8, 4].unpack("nn")` run without checking `length`. If the segment is shorter than 12 bytes, `data[7]` is nil and `.ord` raises NoMethodError. `FastImage#fetch` doesn't rescue NoMethodError, so the exception reaches the caller even with `raise_on_failure: false`. That breaks the gem's promise of returning nil for bad images, and anyone serving a crafted JPEG can trigger it. Check `data.bytesize >= 12` before reading these fields.

The JFIF APP0 values win unconditionally, and the code returns right away without looking at the EXIF APP1 segment. Many cameras and editors write JFIF with units=0 and density 1:1, which means 'unspecified', and put the real DPI in EXIF XResolution/YResolution. Those files will report `[[1, 1], :no_units]` instead of, say, 300 dpi; test3.jpg's new expectation locks this in. JFIF also allows density 0. Fall back to EXIF (or keep scanning) when the JFIF units are 0, at least when the density is 1:1 or 0.

`exif&.x_resolution` uses the safe-navigation operator, which needs Ruby 2.3+. The gemspec declares `required_ruby_version >= 1.9.2`, and the most recent commit specifically restores pre-2.6 compatibility. On older Rubies jpeg.rb won't parse, so the whole gem fails to load. Use `exif && exif.x_resolution && exif.y_resolution`.

`def initialize(stream, parse_resolution: false)` uses keyword arguments, which are a syntax error before Ruby 2.0. The gemspec still advertises `>= 1.9.2`, and Exif is loaded for every user, not only those calling `resolution`. Either use an optional positional argument or raise `required_ruby_version`.

Because the stream is forward-only, any RATIONAL value stored at an offset before the current stream position is silently skipped (`next if skip_amount < 0`). TIFF allows values anywhere in the file, and many writers put the IFD at the end, after the strips and value data. Those TIFFs return nil resolution even though they contain XResolution/YResolution. The new fixture expecting nil for test.dng may be hiding this. At minimum this limitation should be documented; ideally the code should handle it, for example by buffering or noting the values while reading the IFD.

When an image is valid but has no resolution metadata (a PNG without pHYs, any GIF/WebP/SVG, etc.), the parser returns nil and `parse_packets` raises CannotParseImage. With `raise_on_failure: true`, `FastImage.resolution`/`#resolution` therefore raise on perfectly good images instead of returning nil as documented. Because `@resolution` is never assigned in this case, calling `resolution_units` after `resolution` also triggers a second full fetch (another HTTP request), and so does every repeated call. Set `@resolution`/`@resolution_units` to nil explicitly for the resolution property instead of treating it as a parse failure.

Any ResolutionUnit value other than 1 or 3 maps to :inches. That covers the absent-tag default (2), but it also turns invalid or unknown values into :inches. The same pattern is repeated in jpeg.rb:52-56. Consider mapping only nil/2 to :inches and returning :no_units or nil for anything else. Also extract the duplicated mapping into Exif.

XResolution/YResolution are captured only when the field type is RATIONAL (5). Some writers emit SRATIONAL (10), or LONG/SHORT for these tags, and those files return no resolution. The `case type` assignments are also now duplicated across the LONG and SHORT branches, which makes the width/height/orientation handling easier to break later.

Restrict anonymous search to published content. Removing authorization makes `/_emdash/api/search?q=secret&status=draft` accessible anonymously. The schema accepts arbitrary `status` strings, and the route passes that value to `searchWithDb`, whose SQL uses it instead of hardcoding `published`. Consequently, visitors can retrieve draft titles and snippets from search-enabled collections. Force published status for public requests or retain authorization for other statuses.

Atomically claim the initial OAuth administrator. During setup, two OAuth callbacks for different accounts can both read an unset `setup_complete` flag and receive ADMIN privileges. `findOrCreateOAuthUser` creates users without a surrounding transaction, and `finalizeSetup` only sets the flag afterward, so replacing the user-count check with this flag does not prevent the race. Atomically claim initial-admin creation together with the user write so only one callback bypasses domain restrictions.

Resolve the public origin in child sitemaps. Behind a reverse proxy, when the stored site URL is absent but `config.siteUrl` or `EMDASH_SITE_URL` is configured, the sitemap index correctly uses the public origin while this child sitemap emits internal URLs such as `http://localhost:4321/posts/example`. Use `getPublicOrigin(url, emdash.config)` as the fallback here too, keeping indexed content URLs consistent with the sitemap index.

Until `emdash:setup_complete` is set, anyone who finishes GitHub/Google OAuth is created as ADMIN. Nothing ties this to the person running the setup wizard: no setup-session token is checked, the wizard's admin email is ignored, and `/_emdash/api/auth/oauth/*` is public. On a fresh deploy, anyone who reaches the public OAuth endpoints before the operator can take over the site. Before this change, the same callback denied signup because no allowed_domains were configured. Bind first-admin creation to the wizard session (for example a nonce stored in setup_state and carried in OAuth state), or require the OAuth email to match the wizard email.

The AT Protocol callback has the same first-user hole. While setup is incomplete, any DID that finishes the flow becomes ADMIN, and this includes flows started from the public `/_emdash/api/auth/atproto/login`, not only the wizard's setup-admin route. The handle saved in setup_state by `setup-admin.ts` is never compared with the DID that authorized, so the wizard's choice of identity is not enforced. Verify that the callback's DID matches the handle/DID from the setup step before granting Admin.

The PR says first-admin creation 'uses a database transaction to prevent TOCTOU race conditions', but there is no transaction here or in the atproto callback. The comment 'Finalize setup outside the transaction' refers to a transaction that doesn't exist. Two concurrent callbacks can both read setup_complete as unset, and both identities get ADMIN. `finalizeSetup` being idempotent doesn't stop the second admin from being created. Use an atomic claim, such as a conditional insert/update of setup_complete inside a transaction together with createUser.

For the first user, the email is whatever was typed into the setup wizard (setup_state.email, never verified), yet the profile is created with `emailVerified: true`. The user record then claims a verified email the person may not own. That email is trusted by email-based features (magic link, recovery, and auto-linking in `findOrCreateOAuthUser` for later OAuth logins). Set emailVerified to false, or don't use an unverified address.

The client requests `atproto transition:generic`, which grants broad write access to the user's PDS repository. The provider only needs identity. The resulting DPoP keys and refresh tokens are kept indefinitely in `_plugin_storage`: StoredSession has no top-level `expiresAt`, so `createDbStore` never expires it, and nothing deletes the session after login. A database leak would expose write-capable tokens for every admin's Bluesky/AT Protocol account. Request only the `atproto` scope and delete the session after resolving identity.

All the atproto routes (login, callback, setup-admin, client-metadata) build client_id and redirect_uri from `new URL(request.url).origin` rather than `getPublicOrigin()`, which this same change adopts everywhere else for reverse-proxy deployments. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy the origin is `http://localhost:…`, so `isLoopback()` picks the dev loopback client in production, and redirect_uri/client_id point at an internal 127.0.0.1 address. AT Protocol login breaks.

The OAuthClient is a module-level singleton, and its DB stores read the module-global `_currentStorage`, which each request overwrites. With concurrent requests in one isolate, request A's state/session reads and writes can go through request B's Kysely/D1 session binding (the middleware creates per-request D1 sessions). That can cause cross-request I/O errors on Workers or lost read-your-writes consistency. Build the stores per request instead, or pass storage explicitly.
The user's display name is updated in the database before the disabled check runs. A disabled account still modifies its user record on every login attempt. Check `user.disabled` first.

Auth-provider routes are injected even when transparent external auth (e.g. Cloudflare Access) is active, unlike the built-in auth routes, which are skipped. The atproto login/callback routes are also marked public in the middleware. With external auth configured, these routes still accept logins, create users and set Astro sessions, outside the external identity provider. Skip provider route injection under external auth, or reject the configuration.

Any `publicRoutes` prefix declared by a provider descriptor is accepted without validation. A descriptor that declares, for example, `/_emdash/api/` or `/_emdash/admin` silently disables authentication for those paths. Restrict provider public routes to the provider's own namespace (e.g. `/_emdash/api/auth/<id>/`).
`clear()` deletes only the first 10,000 items, so it silently leaves state behind on larger stores. Loop until the query returns no more rows.

Core now lists `@emdash-cms/auth-atproto` as an optional peer dependency, while that package peers on `emdash`. This creates a circular package relationship for a plugin that core never imports. The PR description also documents the import path as `@emdash-cms/plugin-atproto/auth`, but the package actually created is `@emdash-cms/auth-atproto`, so the documented configuration won't resolve.

Handle new-palette requests outside the conditional drawer. When the palettes drawer is hidden, `PaletteTabBar` is not mounted because `ContentView` creates it only when `historyDrawerVisible` is true. Consequently, selecting “New palette…” from the menu has no subscriber and does nothing; the code intended to open the drawer cannot run. Handle this notification in an always-mounted view.

Restore snapshots without recording another history entry. When a named palette is selected, `undo()` and `redo()` reach this code through `applyRestoredSnapshot` and `applyHistoryEntry`. If the restored entry is not the snapshot's first entry, `recordHistory()` inserts it again, pushes another undo snapshot, and clears the redo stack. Thus undo can modify the snapshot it just restored and make redo unavailable. Snapshot restoration should apply colors without recording history.

Include named-palette swaps in the undo snapshot. Swapping a selected chip in a named palette now permanently changes that palette, but `pushUndo()` captures only `autoHistory`, and `undo()` restores only that history. Pressing Undo after the swap therefore leaves the saved chip swapped. Capture and restore the palette being modified, or avoid modifying saved palettes as part of a history-only undoable operation.

Adjust the active index when deleting an earlier palette. With palettes `[History, A, B, C]` and B selected, deleting A leaves `activePaletteIndex` at 2, silently selecting C. Deleting the selected middle palette likewise selects its successor while retaining the old chip selection. Update the index relative to the removed position and explicitly reset selection when the active palette is deleted.

`migrateHistoryToPalettes()` overwrites the palette list with `Defaults[.palettes] = [history]`. It does not merge legacy `colorHistory` into `palettes[0].pairs` as the description says. Any palettes that already exist (for example, from a build where both keys are populated) are silently wiped, including the user's named palettes. It should merge the legacy pairs into `palettes[0]` (dedupe, cap at maxHistory) and keep the other palettes.

`swap()` still calls `pushUndo()` every time, before checking which palette is active. On a named palette, the swap edits the named palette but pushes an auto-history snapshot onto the undo stack and clears the redo stack. Cmd-Z then 'undoes' an unchanged auto-history instead of the swap, and the user's redo history is lost. The description says this was fixed (pushUndo only when the active index is 0), but it was not.

`savePalette` switches `activePaletteIndex` to the new palette but never sets `activeHistoryID = current.id`. The new palette's only chip is not shown as selected, and arrow navigation treats the palette as having no selection. The description says this was fixed, but the change is missing.

`deletePalette` only resets the index when it falls out of range. (1) If you delete a palette before the active one, `activePaletteIndex` is not decremented, so the active tab silently moves to a different palette. (2) When the index is clamped to 0, `restoreAutoHistorySelection()` is never called, so `activeHistoryID` still points at a chip from the deleted palette. The description says both cases were handled, but neither is in the code.

`deleteChipFromPalette` never clears `activeHistoryID` when the removed pair was the active one. The selection keeps pointing at a pair that no longer exists. Swap then quietly does nothing to the palette, and navigation jumps to an end of the list. The description says this was fixed, but the change is missing.

When a named palette is active, `applyEntry` calls `recordHistory()` every time you apply or arrow through a chip. Just browsing a named palette pushes each chip into auto-history and can evict real history past maxHistory. Also, if `recordHistory` returns early because the pair is a duplicate, `lastAutoHistoryID` is set to the named-palette chip's id, not an auto-history id.

`isAutoHistory` is `activePaletteIndex == 0`, but `activePalette` falls back to `palettes.first` when the index is out of range, and nothing clamps the index back. With a stale index, the drawer shows auto-history chips but treats them as a named palette: the '+' button and chip removal call palette methods with an invalid index and do nothing, and Clear History is hidden. The description says `isAutoHistory` is derived from `activePalette?.isAutoHistory` with an async clamp, but neither is implemented.

The chip context menu always shows `textHistoryRemove` ('Remove from history'), even on named palettes. The new `textPaletteRemoveChip` string is never used. The description says the label switches on `isAutoHistory`, but it does not.

A new `ISO8601DateFormatter` is created for every pair inside the `map` closure. These formatters are expensive to create. Create one before the map. The description says this was hoisted, but it was not.
`import Defaults` was added to Exporter, but nothing in the file uses it.

The export filename only lowercases and replaces spaces. A palette name containing '/', ':' or '\' produces an invalid or misleading save-panel filename. `try? json.write` also swallows write errors, so a failed export looks successful. The description says the characters are stripped and errors shown in an NSAlert, but neither is implemented.
Both branches of the ternary are "checkmark.shield", so the icon never changes with state. The active state should use "checkmark.shield.fill", as the description says.
The toolbar tooltips still use the plain strings without keyboard shortcuts. The description says preview (P), compliance (C) and history (H) are included.

Hidden buttons give 'h', 'p' and now 'c' no-modifier shortcuts. SwiftUI key equivalents are handled before the focused text field gets the keystroke. With the new inline `PaletteNameField`, typing a palette name containing these letters toggles compliance or preview, or closes the drawer (which removes the field mid-edit). The new first-responder check in the key monitor only covers the arrow and delete keys. These shortcuts need to be turned off while a palette name is being edited.

The new `.onReceive(.triggerSwap) { angle -= 180 }` stacks with the button action `{ onSwap(); angle -= 180 }`. `onSwap` sends triggerSwap, so a click rotates the icon 360°, ending where it started, and the swap animation looks broken. Remove the `angle -= 180` from the button action now that the notification handles it.

The rename state is keyed by array index (`renamingIndex`), not palette id. If palettes change during a rename (for example, a delete from another tab's context menu), the field and `renamePalette(at:)` apply to whatever palette now sits at that index.
The alert buttons 'Clear' and 'Cancel' are hard-coded, not localized. The export's fallback name "Color History" in Exporter is also not localized, while every other new string goes through PikaText.

Use a matching syntax palette for dark code blocks in light mode. In light mode, this changes code blocks to a dark background while DocFX's syntax highlighter still uses its light-mode token colors. Setting the color on `pre code` does not override colors on highlighted child spans, so dark-colored tokens become difficult to read in the C# examples throughout the documentation. Apply a dark syntax-highlighting palette to these blocks as well, or retain a light background.

This concurrency change isn't mentioned in the PR, which is described as CSS-only. With `cancel-in-progress: true` on the `refs/heads/main` group, a new push to main can cancel a run while `deploy-pages` is publishing. GitHub's Pages starter workflows use `cancel-in-progress: false` for this reason: a cancelled deploy can leave the Pages deployment in a failed or partial state. Also, because the group key is per ref, Pages deploys no longer share one serialized group. If the goal is to cancel stale PR builds, scope cancellation to non-main refs (e.g. `cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}`) and keep the deploy serialized. Otherwise, split this into its own PR.

In light mode, code blocks are forced to a dark background (#1e2530) and only the base `pre code` color is overridden. DocFX's highlight.js token colors (keywords, strings, types, comments) still come from the light highlight theme, which is meant for a light background. Many tokens, such as dark blue keywords and dark green or gray comments, will be very hard to read on the dark steel background. Either keep a light code background in light mode or also override the `.hljs-*` token colors for this dark surface.

The search box uses theme-dependent variables but sits on a navbar that is always dark (`--forge-anvil` is #141a22 in both themes). In dark mode `--forge-steel-light` becomes #c0bbb4 and `--forge-ash` becomes #1a1f28. The result is a bright light-gray input with dark text on the dark navbar, the reverse of light mode and visually broken. Use fixed colors for header elements, as `.navbar-brand` and `thead th` already do.

In light mode the link, inline-code, landing h3 and `td strong` color is #e8760a on a #faf9f7 background. That is about a 2.9:1 contrast ratio, below the WCAG AA 4.5:1 minimum for body text. Combined with `a { text-decoration: none }` at lines 385-389, body links are marked only by a low-contrast color. Use a darker ember for text in light mode (for example around #b45309) and/or keep link underlines.

Nav links, header buttons, including the theme toggle this PR claims to fix, and footer text all use `--forge-smoke` on the fixed #141a22 navbar/footer. In dark mode `--forge-smoke` becomes #6b7280, which is about 3.8:1 contrast on #141a22, below AA for the 0.85-0.875rem text used here. These always-dark surfaces should use a fixed, sufficiently light color instead of the theme-swapped variable.

Fonts are loaded with a CSS `@import` from fonts.googleapis.com. This blocks rendering (the import is only discovered after main.css downloads), adds a runtime dependency on a third-party CDN, and sends visitor IPs to Google, which has been ruled a GDPR problem in some jurisdictions. Consider self-hosting the fonts, or at least using `<link rel=preconnect>`/`<link>` in the template instead of `@import`.

These global `table` rules apply `width: 100%` and `overflow: hidden` to every table, including DocFX's API reference tables. Browsers generally ignore `overflow` on tables, so the rounded corners won't clip the dark header backgrounds as intended. Wide benchmark tables also get no horizontal scrolling of their own. Consider scoping the rules to `article table` and adding a scroll wrapper if needed.

`pre::before` is absolutely positioned inside a `pre` with `overflow: auto`. When a long code line is scrolled horizontally, the ember accent bar scrolls away with the content and the top edge is left bare. Put the accent on a non-scrolling wrapper, or use a `border-top`/`background-image` on the `pre` instead.

Return the updated version after successful lazy rotation. When a read triggers lazy key rotation, the CAS write increments the backing record's version, but its returned record is discarded and `get()` returns the old version. Consequently, a caller that reads a credential and then updates it using `CompareAndSwap { expected_version: fetched.version }` gets a version conflict even without any concurrent writer. Preserve the version and timestamps returned by the successful rotation write while retaining plaintext data in the returned credential.

Lazy re-encryption in `get()` can make the caller's next compare-and-swap fail. When rotation runs, `get()` writes the re-encrypted record with CAS, which bumps the stored version (InMemoryStore sets `expected_version + 1`). But it returns `credential` with the pre-rotation `version`. A caller that reads and then writes back with `PutMode::CompareAndSwap { expected_version: cred.version }` (for example, the resolver's refresh path) gets a spurious `VersionConflict` on the first access after a key rotation. Return the version from the successful rotation `put` (`Ok(stored) => credential.version = stored.version`).

A read now fails when the opportunistic rotation write fails. Plaintext was already decrypted, but any write error other than `VersionConflict` (backend timeout, read-only replica, permission denied) is returned from `get()`. Credential resolution then breaks for every record still on an old key. Rotation is best-effort, so its failures should be logged or ignored, not turned into read failures.

`EncryptionLayer::with_keys` panics through `assert!` when `current_key_id` is missing from `keys`. This is a public library constructor fed by runtime config, and the project rules ban panics in library code. It should return `Result<Self, _>`, or take the current key as a separate argument so the bad state can't be represented. Once that holds, the `current_key()` error path is also dead.

`new` and `with_keys` treat legacy data differently, and the comment on `EncryptedData` is wrong for one of them. `new()` silently aliases `""` to the key, so pre-rotation envelopes (and anything still produced by the public `crypto::encrypt` / `encrypt_with_aad`, which hard-code `key_id = ""`) are readable and get rotated. `with_keys()` has no alias, so the same data fails with "encryption key '' not found". The comment on `EncryptedData::key_id` claims the layer rejects empty key IDs, which is true only for `with_keys`. Moving from single-key to multi-key mode therefore makes un-rotated records unreadable.

Persisted credentials become unreadable and no migration is provided. The state kinds change from `"bearer"` to `"secret_token"` and from `"basic_auth"` to `"identity_password"`, so the resolver's `state_kind` check rejects every existing ApiKey and BasicAuth record with `KindMismatch`. The serialized shape also changes: BasicAuth's `username` field is now `identity`, so old payloads would fail to deserialize anyway. Records stored under the removed `database` and `header_auth` credentials are orphaned. Together with the AAD hard cutover, every existing record needs a migration that this change does not ship. Keep the old kind strings and use `#[serde(alias = "username")]`, or ship a migration.

`resolve_credential` now passes a coarse pattern name (`format!("{:?}", S::pattern())`) as `expected_kind` instead of a type-unique identifier. Many concrete types can share a pattern: every plugin type maps to `Custom`, and any plugin type tagged `SecretToken` matches the built-in `SecretToken`. A resolver that uses `expected_kind` to check compatibility can no longer tell types apart, and mismatch errors can read 'expected SecretToken, got SecretToken'. The `Debug` output of a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum is also being used as a stable wire identifier. Add an explicit `as_str()`, and pass a type-unique key (or `TypeId` / `type_name`) for the scheme check.

`scheme_pattern` replaces `scheme_kind`, which was unique per type, with a lossy category name built from `Debug` formatting. Two different scheme types with the same pattern produce identical snapshots for logging and diagnostics, and `SchemeMismatch` errors can show the same value for `expected` and `actual`. Every `new()`, `project()` failure and `into_project()` failure also allocates a `String` through `format!`. Prefer a `&'static str` from `AuthPattern::as_str()`, plus the concrete `type_name::<S>()` for diagnostics.

The `#[derive(AuthScheme)]` expansion hard-codes `::nebula_core::AuthScheme` and `::nebula_core::AuthPattern`. The derive is re-exported from `nebula_credential` and documented as `use nebula_credential::AuthScheme`, but a plugin crate that depends only on `nebula-credential` or `nebula-sdk` will fail to compile with 'unresolved crate nebula_core'. Emit paths through a re-export the user already has (for example `::nebula_credential::AuthPattern`), or make the crate path configurable.

`key_id` is stored in the envelope but isn't covered by AAD, so it isn't authenticated. Someone who can write to storage can change it to steer which registered key is tried, or to trigger a needless rotate-and-write on read. GCM still blocks decryption with the wrong key, so the impact is limited. Binding `key_id` into the AAD (for example `id || key_id`) would make the envelope tamper-evident.

Testability now has two sources of truth that can disagree: the `TESTABLE` const (still defaults to `false` and is still asserted in tests) and the new `Ok(None)` return from `test()`. A credential can set `TESTABLE = true` and still return `None`, or the reverse, and callers can't tell which one to trust. Drop one of them, or document and enforce that they agree.

Preserve missing newer messages when appending to a jump window. After jumping to an older message, receiving or sending a new message appends it to the partial window. Synchronizing the newer cursor to that message then sets `canLoadNewer` to false, even though messages between the jump window and the new message were never loaded. Those messages become inaccessible through newer pagination. Preserve the contiguous window boundary or load the missing interval before advancing it.

Merge conditional preview classes into the existing class attribute. Blade's `@class` emits a complete `class` attribute, so both this paragraph and the timestamp now render duplicate class attributes. Browsers retain the first attribute and ignore the conditional font/color classes, removing the visual distinction between read and unread previews. Include the static classes in the `@class` expression instead.

pushMessage always adds incoming or sent messages to the end of the loaded window, even when the user has jumped to an older window (canLoadNewer === true). This leaves a gap between the old window and the new message. syncCursorsFromFlat then moves newerId/newerCreatedAt to the pushed message, so the next loadNewer only fetches messages newer than it. Every message in the gap is skipped for good, and the user never sees them. sendMessage/sendLike also dispatch scroll-bottom, which drops the user at a discontinuous timeline. When canLoadNewer is true before the push, reload the latest window with loadLatestWindow() instead of appending.

The early return in loadOlder (canLoadOlder false or cursors missing) does not dispatch 'older-loaded'. The client's loadOlderWithStableScroll sets pendingPrependRestore = true, and only the older-loaded handler clears it. If the client's $wire.canLoadOlder is stale, this path is hit, pendingPrependRestore and loadingOlder both stay true, and isNearTop() returns false from then on, so the top of the chat can never load again. The same lock-up happens if the Livewire call never settles. Dispatch older-loaded on every exit path, or clear the flags in a finally block on the client.

loadingOlder is only reset when older-loaded fires before the await resolves, or in the catch block. A failed request in Livewire usually does not reject the $wire promise, and a missing event leaves the guard stuck (see loadOlder). The PR description promises a try/finally guard (`loadingMore` with `finally { this.loadingMore = false }`) around `$wire.loadMore()`, but the code uses a different, more fragile scheme and different names. Either the description is stale or the intended change was never committed.

The previous waitForMedia() logic, which waited for every img/video to load before scrolling to the bottom and revealing the chat, was replaced with fixed 100ms/220ms timers. onAnyMediaLoad only scrolls to the bottom while `initializing` is true. Images or videos that finish loading after 220ms (any normal network) push content down, and the conversation opens above the latest messages. This is a regression for chats with media.

pushMessage and removeMessage now call syncCanLoadFlags, which runs two EXISTS queries each time. The attachment send loop calls pushMessage once per uploaded file, so sending N attachments costs 2N extra queries, and every realtime message adds two more. Append-only paths can sync once after the loop, or skip the older check, because appending never changes canLoadOlder. The PR description claims this resync work was reduced, but the code adds it.

Removing x-persist="chats" from the sidebar, here and in pages/chats.blade.php, means every wire:navigate between conversations re-mounts the Chats component. That re-runs its queries, throws away conversations already loaded via loadMore, and resets the sidebar scroll position. This is a noticeable UX and performance regression for a core package flow, and the description does not justify it.

`wire:navigate:scroll` is not a Livewire directive. Livewire's scroll preservation for wire:navigate is `wire:scroll`, and it only applies inside persisted (x-persist) elements, which this PR removes. The attribute does nothing, so the claimed scroll-restoration fix for the chat list never happens.

Now that the sidebar is no longer persisted, this x-init runs again on every navigation and adds another document 'livewire:navigated' listener each time without removing the old ones. Listeners pile up and hold references to detached containers, so each navigation fires a growing number of scrollToConversation retry loops.

The Chats component already subscribes to the NotifyParticipant echo event through its getListeners (refreshComponent). Calling Livewire.dispatch('refresh-chats') here makes a second refresh round-trip for every notification. This script is also only injected when web push notifications are enabled, so it cannot be what keeps unread state in sync for panels without web push.

Nothing in the package dispatches 'open-attachment', yet it is mapped to jumpToMessage(int $messageId). If wirechat-pro or a user app dispatches an event with that name and a different payload (for example attachment data), the listener will throw a TypeError or rebuild the message window unexpectedly. Opening an attachment also has nothing to do with jumping the timeline, so use a dedicated event name.
totalMessageCount and paginate_var are no longer used for pagination, but a full COUNT query still runs on every mount. Drop it, or keep the public property without running the query.

removeDeletedMessage, the realtime delete from a peer, still edits loadedMessages directly and does not resync cursors or canLoad flags like removeMessage now does. Deleting the last loaded message can therefore leave canLoadOlder/canLoadNewer stale and empty groups out of sync with the new window bookkeeping.
The change commits modified macOS .DS_Store files (root, .github, database, lang, resources, src, tests). They should be removed from the repo and added to .gitignore.
The new tests use sleep(1) to separate timestamps, which slows the suite by several seconds. Use Carbon::setTestNow or travel() instead.
